## Verdict
- Answer: The evidence that higher rates lower house prices is strong in direction but modest and variable in size. Mortgage-rate and monetary-policy shocks reduce prices in most studies, but the magnitudes depend on the country, the period and supply conditions. Raw time series often contradict the effect because incomes, supply and expectations move at the same time.
- Decision: Treat rate rises as a real downside risk to prices and plan around a range, not a point forecast. Do not assume a fixed pass-through such as "1 point of rate means X% of price".
- Confidence: medium - the causal literature is consistent in sign, but the effect sizes in this document come from memory (est.), and no Prism call was run.
- What would change it: Run the Prism evidence and counter-evidence calls to count and tier-weight the literature, and fetch local price and rate series for the market in question.

## What the data shows
No Prism calls were run. Every figure below is an estimate from memory (est.) and should be verified before use. The data cannot answer these facets:
- Volumes by corpus and lane: no corpus counts were retrieved.
- Tier-weighted tally and read/unread counts: not measured. Nothing was read in full; all claims are recalled from memory.
- News versus research series: no series was retrieved.

Recalled findings:
- Monetary-policy shocks: a 1 percentage point surprise rise in the policy rate lowers real house prices by roughly 1–4% within 1–3 years in VAR-based studies of advanced economies (est.). Estimates vary widely by method and country.
- US mortgage rates: the 30-year fixed rate rose from about 3% in early 2021 to about 7% in late 2023 (est.). Nominal US prices did not fall nationally. The Case-Shiller national index fell only about 3–4% from mid-2022 to early 2023 and then recovered (est.). The "lock-in" effect, in which owners with cheap mortgages do not sell, cut supply and propped up prices (est.).
- UK: after the 2022 mini-budget, prices fell roughly 3–5% from the 2022 peak (est.).
- Canada, New Zealand and Sweden: these saw larger falls of about 10–25% from peak (est.), and Sweden's fall was at the high end. Variable-rate exposure and high debt-to-income ratios are the likely reasons.
- Long-run comparison: in the 1980s and 2000s, real prices fell after tightening in some countries but not others (est.).
